topic.title: Quartiles and interquartile range from a list
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One short question of its own on most M3 papers (2 to 3 marks, often a bare list of 9 to 11 values), and the engine behind the quartile parts of the cumulative frequency and box plot questions later in the paper. Examined again in M4, M7 and M8.
mustMemorise: Order the data first; a quartile is a position, not a value you can spot
Lower quartile at position ¼(n + 1), median at ½(n + 1), upper quartile at ¾(n + 1)
A fractional position means the value that fraction of the way between its two neighbours
Interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartile, in the units of the data
notOnThisSpec: Standard deviation and variance: the CCEA specification names no measure of dispersion beyond the range and the interquartile range
Deciles and percentiles: only quartiles appear in the M3 statements
A formal outlier test such as 1.5 × IQR: CCEA asks you to notice an extreme value, never to test for one

note.title: Quartiles and the interquartile range from a list
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: lower quartile at position ¼(n + 1) of the ordered data
interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartile

notOnThisSpec: Standard deviation and variance: the CCEA specification names no measure of dispersion beyond the range and the interquartile range
Deciles and percentiles: only quartiles appear in the M3 statements
A formal outlier test such as 1.5 × IQR: CCEA asks you to notice an extreme value, never to test for one

mustBeAbleTo: Put an unordered list into size order before anything else is counted
Work out the three quartile positions from n, and say what a position of 2.5 or 10.5 means
Read the lower quartile, median and upper quartile off the ordered list
Subtract to get the interquartile range and write it with the units of the data
Work backwards from a quartile and the interquartile range to the other quartile
Say what a smaller interquartile range means about a data set, in the words of the context
Choose between the range and the interquartile range and justify the choice by naming the extreme value in the data
sheet.howExamined: A short question in the second half of the M3 paper, worth 2 or 3 marks, usually a printed list of 9 to 11 values with a single instruction such as 'Calculate the interquartile range'. The scheme gives one mark for the two quartiles and one for the subtraction, so a correct pair with a slip in the subtraction still scores. The same skill returns inside the cumulative frequency and box plot questions, where the quartiles come off a graph instead of a list.
traps: The list is printed out of order and the positions are counted along it as printed; every quartile then comes from the wrong value
The range is offered where the interquartile range was asked for (Summer 2024 M3 Q26: the interquartile range was unfamiliar to many)
A position of 2.5 or 10.5 is rounded to a whole number instead of being read as halfway between two values
Only half the box is measured: the median is subtracted from the upper quartile
The position is written on the answer line instead of the value at that position
A 'why is the interquartile range better' answer is given as a memorised rule with nothing from the data (November 2025 M3 Q26(b) was the poorest response on that paper)

Reading quartiles off an axis marked in thousands and then writing the bare numbers down: the subtraction still earns its method mark, but the interquartile range has to carry the units the axis was labelled in (Summer 2025 M3 Q24)

workedExamples.stem:
A post office recorded how long, in minutes, each of eleven customers waited to be served:

6, 2, 9, 4, 11, 3, 7, 5, 14, 8, 5

Work out the interquartile range of the waiting times. [3]

figure.alt: The eleven waiting times written in order from 2 to 14 minutes and numbered 1 to 11, with markers under position 3 for the lower quartile, position 6 for the median and position 9 for the upper quartile.

steps.decision: Nothing else can start until the values are ordered. A quartile is a position in the ordered data, so an unordered list gives a quartile from the wrong place.

options: Because a quartile is defined by where a value sits in the ordered data
Because the largest value has to come last on the answer line
Because the mean changes when the order changes
whyMenu.explain: Ordering is what turns a list into a ranking, and the quartiles are positions in that ranking.

steps.working: $n = 11$. Lower quartile position $\tfrac{1}{4}(11 + 1) = 3$; upper quartile position $\tfrac{3}{4}(11 + 1) = 9$.
steps.decision: The positions are written down before any value is read. With eleven values both positions are whole numbers, so no averaging is needed.

steps.working: The 3rd value is $4$ and the 9th value is $9$.
steps.decision: Count along the ordered list, not the original one. Both quartiles are recorded before subtracting.
Upper quartile minus lower quartile, in the units of the data. Writing the units on the answer line costs nothing and protects the accuracy mark.

twin.stem:
The next morning eleven more customers were timed, in minutes:

9, 4, 12, 6, 15, 5, 10, 7, 18, 11, 8

Work out the interquartile range. [3]

workedExamples.stem:
Nine bags of seed potatoes are weighed. Their masses, in kilograms, are

23, 15, 34, 12, 28, 18, 25, 14, 20

Work out the interquartile range of the masses. [3]

figure.alt: The nine masses in order from 12 to 34 kilograms and numbered 1 to 9, with markers at position 2.5, position 5 and position 7.5; the quartile markers sit between two boxes.

steps.decision: Order first, then count how many values there are, because every position comes from $n$.
Neither position is a whole number this time. A position of 2.5 means halfway between the 2nd and 3rd values, which is their mean.

options: Because position 2.5 lies halfway between positions 2 and 3, so the value halfway between them is used
Because 2.5 rounds up to 3, so the 3rd value is used
Because a decimal position means the data set is too small for quartiles
whyMenu.explain: A fractional position is read the same way a point between two marks on a ruler is read: go the stated fraction of the way from one value to the next.

steps.decision: Both quartiles are written down in full before subtracting, so a slip in one of them is still visible to the marker.
The answer is a width, so it carries the units of the masses.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Interquartile range 12 kg (LQ 14.5 kg, UQ 26.5 kg).

Work out the interquartile range. [3]

items.stem: A list of 11 ordered values is given. At which position is the lower quartile?
items.skill: Use the CCEA quartile positions for a list

options.feedback: That is $\tfrac{n}{4}$. CCEA's rule adds one first: $\tfrac{1}{4}(n + 1)$.
Position 4 would be $\tfrac{1}{4}(11 + 5)$. The rule is $\tfrac{1}{4}(n + 1) = 3$.
The 6th value is the median, $\tfrac{1}{2}(11 + 1)$. The lower quartile is at position 3.

items.stem: A question gives eight masses that are not in size order and asks for the interquartile range. What is the first thing to do?
items.skill: Order the data before any position is counted

options.text: Write the masses out again from smallest to largest
options.feedback: Yes. Every quartile is a position in the ordered data, so ordering comes first.

options.text: Subtract the smallest mass from the largest
options.feedback: That gives the range. The interquartile range needs the two quartiles of the ordered list.

options.text: Count to the 2nd and 6th masses as they are printed
options.feedback: Counting along the printed list reads the quartiles from the wrong values. Order them first.

options.text: Add the masses and divide by eight
options.feedback: That is the mean, which is not asked for here and does not need ordering at all.

items.stem: Seven plants have heights, in centimetres, of 4, 9, 6, 12, 7, 10, 5. What is the interquartile range?
items.skill: Find the interquartile range of a short list

options.feedback: In order the heights are $4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12$; LQ $= 5$, UQ $= 10$, so the IQR is $5$ cm.
That is the range. The interquartile range describes the middle half only.
That is the distance from the median to the upper quartile, half of what was asked for.
That is the median. The interquartile range is upper quartile minus lower quartile.

items.stem: Two netball squads have the same median height. Squad A has an interquartile range of 4 cm and squad B has one of 11 cm. What does that tell you?
items.skill: Interpret the size of an interquartile range

options.text: The middle half of squad A's heights are closer together, so squad A is more consistent
options.feedback: Yes. A smaller interquartile range means less variation in the middle half.

options.text: Squad A is taller on average
options.feedback: The medians are equal, so neither squad is taller on average. The interquartile range describes spread, not average.
The interquartile range says nothing about how many players there are; it measures the width of the middle half.

options.text: Squad B has the taller tallest player
options.feedback: That would be a statement about the range. The interquartile range never reaches the extreme values.

items.stem: In an ordered list of nine values the largest value is changed from 12 to 40. Which of these changes?
items.skill: Know that quartiles resist extreme values

options.feedback: Yes. The quartiles are at positions 2.5 and 7.5, so the ninth value never enters them; only the range moves.

options.text: The range and the interquartile range
options.feedback: The interquartile range comes from positions 2.5 and 7.5, so the largest value is outside it.
The median is the 5th value, which has not moved. The range is the one that changes.
The range is largest minus smallest, so it grows by 28.

items.stem: A list has 13 values in order. Where is the upper quartile?
items.skill: Handle a quartile position that is not a whole number

options.feedback: Yes: $\tfrac{3}{4}(13 + 1) = 10.5$, so take the mean of the 10th and 11th values.
Position 10.5 is not rounded down. Take the mean of the values at positions 10 and 11.
Position 10.5 is not rounded up either; it is halfway between the two.
That is $\tfrac{3n}{4}$. CCEA's position is $\tfrac{3}{4}(n + 1) = 10.5$.

context.setting: Minutes spent queueing at seven tills in a shop

parts.stem:
Seven customers were timed at a till. Their times, in minutes, were

14, 9, 21, 12, 17, 10, 25

Find the median time.
hints: Put the seven times in order from smallest to largest first.
With $n = 7$ the median sits at position $\tfrac{1}{2}(7 + 1) = 4$.
Count along the ordered list to that position and read the value there.
parts.workedSolution: In order: $9, 10, 12, 14, 17, 21, 25$. The median position is $\tfrac{1}{2}(7 + 1) = 4$, so the median is the 4th value, $14$ minutes.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the middle of the list as it was printed. The times have to be put in order first; then the fourth value is the median.
That is the position, not the time. Position 4 tells you where to look; the answer is the value you find there.

context.setting: Masses of seven parcels weighed at a post office counter

parts.stem:
The masses, in kilograms, of seven parcels are

3.2, 1.5, 4.8, 2.6, 6.1, 2, 3.9

Find the lower quartile.
hints: Order the masses first.
The lower quartile sits at position $\tfrac{1}{4}(7 + 1) = 2$.
parts.workedSolution: In order: $1.5, 2, 2.6, 3.2, 3.9, 4.8, 6.1$. Lower quartile position $\tfrac{1}{4}(7 + 1) = 2$, so LQ $= 2$ kg.

commonErrors.feedback: The second mass of the printed list is not the lower quartile. Order the seven masses, then count to position 2.

parts.stem: Find the upper quartile.
hints: The upper quartile sits at position $\tfrac{3}{4}(7 + 1) = 6$.
parts.workedSolution: Upper quartile position $\tfrac{3}{4}(7 + 1) = 6$, so UQ $= 4.8$ kg.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the sixth mass of the printed list. Count to position 6 of the ordered list instead.

context.setting: Eggs collected each day from a small henhouse

parts.stem:
A henhouse was checked on eleven mornings. The numbers of eggs collected were

18, 25, 21, 29, 19, 24, 34, 22, 27, 20, 31

Work out the interquartile range.

scheme.for: lower quartile 20 and upper quartile 29 both identified

hints: Order the eleven counts.
$\tfrac{1}{4}(11 + 1) = 3$ and $\tfrac{3}{4}(11 + 1) = 9$, so both quartiles are whole positions.
Interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartile.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the range, largest minus smallest. The interquartile range uses the two quartiles, so it describes the middle half only.
You have measured from the median up to the upper quartile, which is only half of the spread you were asked for. Subtract the lower quartile, not the median.

context.setting: Heights of nine tomato seedlings in a greenhouse

parts.stem:
The heights, in centimetres, of nine seedlings are

7, 11, 9, 15, 8, 13, 18, 10, 16

Write down the position of the lower quartile.
hints: Use $\tfrac{1}{4}(n + 1)$ with $n = 9$.
parts.workedSolution: $\tfrac{1}{4}(9 + 1) = 2.5$, so the lower quartile lies halfway between the 2nd and 3rd heights.

commonErrors.feedback: You used $\tfrac{n}{4}$. CCEA's position is $\tfrac{1}{4}(n + 1)$, which is 2.5 here, so the quartile sits halfway between two values.

parts.stem: Find the lower quartile.
hints: Order the heights first.
Position 2.5 means halfway between the 2nd and 3rd heights, so take their mean.
parts.workedSolution: In order: $7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16, 18$. Position 2.5 sits between $8$ and $9$, so LQ $= \dfrac{8 + 9}{2} = 8.5$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: You kept the median inside the lower half and took the middle of five heights. The position rule gives 2.5, which is the mean of the 2nd and 3rd heights.
That is the position from part (a). Go to that place in the ordered list and read the height.

Find the median distance.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the seventh number as printed. Order the thirteen distances, then count to position 7.

parts.stem: Work out the interquartile range of the distances.

hints: Each quartile is the mean of the two distances it sits between.

context.setting: Minutes by which eleven morning trains were delayed at a halt

parts.stem:
Eleven morning trains were recorded as leaving late by these numbers of minutes:

3, 5, 4, 6, 5, 7, 4, 8, 6, 5, 58

Work out the range.
hints: Range = largest value − smallest value.
parts.workedSolution: Largest $58$, smallest $3$, so the range is $58 - 3 = 55$ minutes.

parts.stem: Work out the interquartile range.

scheme.for: lower quartile 4 and upper quartile 7 both identified

hints: Order the delays, then use positions 3 and 9.
The 58 stays in the list; it just does not reach either quartile.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the range, and it is driven entirely by the one train that was 58 minutes late. The interquartile range leaves that train outside the middle half.
You stopped at the median. The interquartile range is upper quartile minus lower quartile.

parts.stem: State which of the two measures better describes the spread of a typical delay at this halt. Give a reason for your answer.

accepted: The interquartile range, because the one delay of 58 minutes is extreme and it stretches the range without saying anything about a typical morning
The interquartile range, because the 58 minute delay is an outlier and the range is distorted by it

scheme.for: the interquartile range, with a reason that names the 58-minute delay as an extreme value that inflates the range
reject: the interquartile range is better (no reason)
the IQR ignores extremes (no reference to this data)
scheme.examinerNote: A memorised contrast of range and IQR with nothing from this data set does not score.

hints: Look at what one value does to each measure.
Say which measure you choose and name the value that causes the trouble.
parts.workedSolution: The interquartile range. Ten of the eleven delays are between 3 and 8 minutes, but one train was 58 minutes late, and that single value fixes the range at 55 minutes. The interquartile range of 3 minutes describes the middle half and is not moved by that one train.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the general rule rather than a reason about these delays. The mark comes from naming the 58-minute train and saying that it stretches the range.

context.setting: Two machines filling 500 g bags of oats

parts.stem:
Two machines fill bags of oats. Eleven bags from each machine are weighed.

Machine P (g): 498, 502, 499, 501, 500, 503, 497, 502, 500, 499, 501

Machine Q (g): 505, 492, 499, 510, 488, 501, 495, 503, 497, 507, 500

Work out the interquartile range for machine P.

scheme.for: lower quartile 499 and upper quartile 502 both identified (g)

hints: Order machine P's eleven masses.
Quartiles at positions 3 and 9.

commonErrors.feedback: That is machine P's range. Use the two quartiles instead so that the comparison is about the middle half of the bags.

parts.stem: Work out the interquartile range for machine Q.

scheme.for: lower quartile 495 and upper quartile 505 both identified (g)

hints: Order machine Q's eleven masses.
Quartiles at positions 3 and 9 again.

commonErrors.feedback: That is machine Q's range. The interquartile range is upper quartile minus lower quartile.

parts.stem: State which machine fills the bags more consistently. Give a reason for your answer.

accepted: Machine P, because its interquartile range of 3 g is smaller than machine Q's 10 g, so the middle half of its bags vary less
Machine P, because 3 g is a smaller interquartile range than 10 g so its masses are closer together

reject: machine q fills the bags more

scheme.for: machine P, because its interquartile range (3 g) is smaller than machine Q's (10 g)
reject: machine P with no comparison of the two interquartile ranges

hints: Consistent means the masses are close together.
Quote both interquartile ranges in your sentence.
parts.workedSolution: Machine P. Its interquartile range is $3$ g against machine Q's $10$ g, so the middle half of machine P's bags are much closer together and it is the more consistent machine.

commonErrors.feedback: The choice is right, but the mark needs the evidence. Add the two interquartile ranges and say that the smaller one means less variation.

parts.stem:
For a set of data the lower quartile is 27 and the interquartile range is 19.

Work out the upper quartile.
hints: IQR = UQ − LQ, so UQ = LQ + IQR.

commonErrors.feedback: You subtracted. The upper quartile is above the lower quartile, so the interquartile range is added on.

parts.stem:
For a second set of data the upper quartile is 62 and the interquartile range is 23.

Work out the lower quartile.
hints: Rearrange IQR = UQ − LQ to LQ = UQ − IQR.

commonErrors.feedback: You added. The lower quartile is below the upper quartile, so the interquartile range is taken off.

context.setting: Minutes spent on the school bus by fifteen pupils in a class

figures.alt: The fifteen bus times in order from 8 to 35 minutes, numbered 1 to 15, with markers under position 4 for the lower quartile, position 8 for the median and position 12 for the upper quartile.

parts.stem:
Fifteen pupils recorded how long, in minutes, their bus journey to school took one morning:

8, 22, 15, 30, 12, 18, 25, 10, 20, 35, 14, 28, 16, 24, 19

Find the median time.
hints: Order the fifteen times first.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the eighth time as printed. The list has to be ordered before any position is counted.

parts.stem: Work out the interquartile range of the times.

scheme.for: lower quartile 14 and upper quartile 25 both identified

hints: Positions 4 and 12.
IQR = UQ − LQ.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the range of the fifteen times. The interquartile range measures the middle half.
You measured from the median to the upper quartile. Subtract the lower quartile instead.

parts.stem:
A second class recorded their bus times. Their median was 19 minutes and their interquartile range was 19 minutes.

Compare the bus times of the two classes.

accepted: The medians are the same, so on average the journeys are equally long, but this class has a smaller interquartile range so its times are more consistent
Both medians are 19 minutes, so the typical journey is the same, and the smaller interquartile range here means less variation than in the second class

scheme.for: one statement about the averages (equal medians) and one about the spread (this class has the smaller interquartile range, so it is more consistent)
scheme.examinerNote: Quoting the four numbers with no interpretation does not score; the comparison has to say what they mean.

hints: Compare one average and one measure of spread.
Say what the difference in the interquartile ranges means about the journeys.
parts.workedSolution: Both medians are $19$ minutes, so on average the two classes travel for the same time. This class has an interquartile range of $11$ minutes against the other class's $19$ minutes, so its journey times are more consistent.

commonErrors.feedback: The numbers are right, but a comparison has to say what they mean: which is more spread out, and what that says about the journeys.

context.setting: Masses of nine items posted by a small office, one of them a parcel

parts.stem:
An office posted nine items one morning. Their masses, in grams, were

22, 35, 28, 40, 31, 26, 38, 33, 180

Work out the range of the masses.
hints: Range = largest − smallest.

parts.stem: Work out the interquartile range of the masses.

scheme.for: lower quartile 27 and upper quartile 39 both identified (g)

hints: With $n = 9$ the quartile positions are 2.5 and 7.5.
Each quartile is the mean of the two masses it sits between.

commonErrors.feedback: That is part (a) again. The interquartile range comes from the two quartiles, so the 180 g parcel never enters the calculation.
The fifth mass was counted into both halves. Use the positions 2.5 and 7.5 on the whole ordered list.

parts.stem: Explain why the interquartile range describes the masses of these items better than the range does.

accepted: The 180 g parcel is far heavier than everything else and it alone fixes the range at 158 g, while the interquartile range describes the middle half and is not moved by it
One item of 180 g is extreme, so the range is stretched by a single mass, but the interquartile range uses only the middle half

scheme.for: names the 180 g item as the extreme value that inflates the range, and says the interquartile range uses the middle half only
reject: the range is affected by extremes (no reference to the 180 g item)
scheme.examinerNote: November 2025 M3 Q26(b) was the poorest-answered item on that paper: generic contrasts of range and IQR earned nothing, and the mark needed the extreme value of this data set.

hints: Look at the nine masses and find the one that is not like the others.
Say what that value does to the range, and why the interquartile range escapes it.
parts.workedSolution: Eight of the nine masses lie between $22$ g and $40$ g, but one parcel is $180$ g. That single item fixes the range at $158$ g, which describes no typical letter. The interquartile range of $12$ g measures the middle half of the items and is untouched by the parcel.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rule in general, and examiners did not accept it. Point at the 180 g parcel in this list and say that the range is stretched by it.

findTheMistake.stem: Nine pupils timed how long, in minutes, they took to walk home: 12, 7, 15, 9, 20, 11, 17, 8, 14. Orla was asked for the interquartile range. Here is her working.
studentWorking: $n = 9$, so the quartiles are at positions 2.5 and 7.5.
Position 2.5: halfway between $7$ and $15$, so LQ $= 11$.
Position 7.5: halfway between $17$ and $8$, so UQ $= 12.5$.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The positions in line 1 are right, but they were counted along the times as they were written down rather than along the ordered list. Line 3 repeats the same slip, and line 4 inherits both, so the final width is smaller than the real one.
findTheMistake.feedback: As written this scores 1 of 3. The position rule in line 1 earns its mark, but both quartiles come from the unordered list, so the accuracy marks go. Ordering the nine times first gives LQ 8.5, UQ 16 and an interquartile range of 7.5 minutes.

prompts.prompt: Where is the lower quartile of an ordered list of n values?
Where is the upper quartile of an ordered list of n values?
What must be done to a list of values before any quartile is found?
prompts.answer: Put the values in order, smallest to largest.

prompts.prompt: A quartile position works out as 3.5. What value do you write down?
prompts.answer: The value halfway between the 3rd and 4th values of the ordered list, that is, their mean.

prompts.prompt: What does a small interquartile range tell you about a data set?
prompts.answer: The middle half of the values are close together, so the data is more consistent.

prompts.prompt: Why is the interquartile range often preferred to the range?
prompts.answer: The range is fixed by the two extreme values, so a single unusual value can stretch it; the interquartile range uses only the middle half.

prompts.prompt: The lower quartile is 14 and the interquartile range is 9. What is the upper quartile?
